analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders to publicly name who funds their campaign ads.
analysis.headline: The DISCLOSE 2015 Act drew 132 Democratic House sponsors but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced corporations, labor unions, tax-exempt groups, and super PACs that spend more than $10,000 a year on campaign advertising to report that spending to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, and to name anyone who gave them $10,000 or more for it. TV ads would have had to show their top five funders on screen and radio ads their top two, and corporate CEOs or union presidents would have had to appear on camera saying they approve the message. It also would have expanded the window of time before an election when such ads count as regulated 'electioneering communications,' and required registered lobbyists to report their own independent spending.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would learn the actual names behind ads that attack or promote candidates. Shareholders and union members would learn how the organizations they own or belong to are spending money on politics, since covered groups would have to include that spending in their regular reports and link to it from their websites.

how_it_helps.text: Covered organizations spending over $10,000 a year on campaign-related ads would have to file a statement with the FEC within 24 hours of crossing that threshold, listing each disbursement over $1,000 and identifying the candidate supported or opposed [S3].

Any person or organization that gave a covered group $10,000 or more toward campaign spending would be named, with dates and amounts, unless they gave in writing that the money not be used for politics [S3].

Television ads paid for with covered political spending would carry a 'Top Five Funders' list on screen for at least 6 seconds and radio ads a 'Top Two Funders' list, and the highest-ranking official of the paying group would have to approve the message by name [S3].

Corporations, unions, and tax-exempt groups that send regular reports to shareholders, members, or donors would have to include their political spending in those reports and post a link to their FEC filings on their homepage [S3].
Registered lobbyists would have to report any independent expenditure or electioneering communication of $1,000 or more, naming each candidate and whether the spending supported or opposed them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, 501(c)(4) and other tax-exempt groups, and super PACs would bear new reporting costs and, more significantly, the loss of anonymity for their large donors. Wealthy individuals who currently fund campaign advertising through intermediaries would see their names disclosed once their giving crossed $10,000 a year.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real compliance burdens: 24-hour filing deadlines, per-disbursement reports above $1,000, and on-screen funder lists that could crowd out ad content for shorter spots, with the FEC allowed to waive the list only for hardship [S3].

Critics of donor disclosure have long argued, citing cases like NAACP v. Alabama, that naming supporters can expose them to harassment or retaliation, which is a good-faith concern even though this bill sets the threshold at $10,000 rather than naming small donors [S3].
Disclosure alone does not limit the money itself: the bill caps no spending and imposes no contribution limits, so the volume of political money would be unchanged, only better labeled [S3].
An unrelated provision repeals the existing ban on political contributions by individuals age 17 or younger, a change unconnected to the disclosure scheme [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters, the benefit is straightforward: ads attacking candidates would carry the actual names of the people paying for them, ending much of what is commonly called dark money. The costs fall on the organizations doing the spending, in paperwork and in the loss of donor anonymity, and the harassment concern is real but mitigated by the $10,000 floor. The bill's main design weakness is that it relies on disclosure alone; it would not slow the money, only label it, and enforcement would depend entirely on an FEC with a record of deadlock.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2015 and referred to three committees; after one subcommittee referral in February 2015, no committee ever acted on it and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Van Hollen introduced the DISCLOSE 2015 Act in the House on January 21, 2015 [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means Committees [S5].
On February 5, 2015, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice; that is the last action recorded in the Congress [S5].
It accumulated 131 cosponsors, all Democrats, in addition to the sponsor [S4].

The bill would have required covered organizations spending over $10,000 a year on campaign activity to report the spending and their large funders to the FEC within 24 hours, and would have required funder lists on broadcast ads [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organizations that spend on campaigns without naming their funders — corporations, tax-exempt 501(c)(4) groups, and super PACs — kept the status quo, and the voters who would have learned the funders' names did not. The House Republican majority was never asked to take a position on the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 132 sponsors were House Democrats and the record shows no Republican cosponsor; with Republicans holding the House majority and controlling the calendar, the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Corporations and trade associations funding campaign ads
industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to fund candidate ads through intermediaries without naming funders, requiring 24-hour FEC reporting and top-funder lists on ads. Voters would see who was behind the messaging.

These groups are the main vehicle for undisclosed political spending, and the bill defined them as covered organizations, requiring them to disclose large funders and post their FEC filings online. Their core advantage — anonymity — would have disappeared.

industries.industry: Super PACs and political committees taking unlimited money
industries.note: Committees accepting unlimited donations would face reporting on those accounts, and their ads would carry funder lists and CEO or union-president approval statements. They could still raise and spend without limits; only the labeling would change.

Unions are covered organizations under the bill, so they would face the same 24-hour reporting and ad funder lists as corporations, a real administrative burden — though the bill gives them and their members symmetric transparency with corporate spenders.

Anyone giving $10,000 or more toward campaign spending through a covered group would be named, with amounts and dates, unless they directed in writing that the money not be used for politics. Wealthy donors funding ads through nonprofits would lose their anonymity.
